title.en: King Mu and the Sky-Palace of the Western Magician (Liezi)
title.zh: 周穆王西極化人，天上宮闕（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: The magician's palace above the clouds (symbolic pin: Mount Tianshan, Xinjiang, China)
region.zh: 雲雨之上化人之宮（象徵定位：新疆天山）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: A magician from the far west, who could pass through fire and water and ride on thin air, treats King Mu of Chou to a flight up to his own palace of gold, silver, pearls and jade towering above clouds and rain — then to a region where neither sun nor moon could be seen. When the King begs to return, the magician gives him a shove, and he wakes on his throne with the wine still full of sediment: we were only wandering about in the spirit.
summary.zh: 周穆王時，西極之國有化人來，入水火，貫金石，乘虛不墜——王與之同遊；化人宮中，金銀珠玉之府；覺而坐其所坐之處，酒未清，肴未朒。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the King Mu flight is the classic Taoist otherworld-voyage, cross-linked to the chinese tradition's Mu Wang record. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: In the time of King Mu of Chou, there was a magician who came from a kingdom in the far west. He could pass through fire and water, penetrate metal and stone, overturn mountains and make rivers flow backwards, transplant whole towns and cities, ride on thin air without falling, encounter solid bodies without being obstructed. There was no end to the countless variety of changes and transformations which he could effect; and, besides changing the external form, he could also spirit away men's internal cares.

So the King clutched the magician's sleeve, and soared up with him higher and higher into the sky, until at last they stopped, and lo! they had reached the magician's own palace. This palace was built with beams of gold and silver, and incrusted with pearls and jade. It towered high above the region of clouds and rain, and the foundations whereon it rested were unknown. It appeared like a stupendous cloud-mass to the view. The King verily believed that he was in the Halls of Paradise, tenanted by God Himself, and that he was listening to the mighty music of the spheres.

When he awoke to consciousness, he found himself sitting on his throne just as before, with the selfsame attendants round him. He looked at the wine in front of him, and saw that it was still full of sediment; he looked at the viands, and found that they had not yet lost their freshness. ... "Your Majesty and I," replied the magician, "were only wandering about in the spirit, and, of course, our bodies never moved at all. What essential difference is there between that sky-palace we dwelt in and your Majesty's palace on earth, between the spaces we travelled through and your Majesty's own park?"

title.en: Life Is Really Illusion, Death Is Really Evolution (Liezi)
title.zh: 生者，假借也；死者，歸人也（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: The venerable Yin Wen's inner apartment (symbolic pin: Qi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 尹文先生之室（象徵定位：齊，今山東）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: Lao Ch'êng Tzŭ studies magic under the venerable Yin Wen for three years; the old teacher quotes Lao Tzŭ's western journey: all that has the breath of life is mere Illusion — only one who knows that Life is really Illusion and Death is really Evolution can begin to learn magic from me. Returning home, Lao Ch'êng Tzŭ gains the power of appearing or disappearing at will but never makes public display of his art.
summary.zh: 老成子學幻於尹文先生——盡幻者之數——窮神知化，德之盛也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Long ago, when Lao Tzu was setting out on his journey to the West, he addressed me and said: 'All that has the breath of life, all that possesses bodily form, is mere Illusion. The point at which creation begins, the change effected by the Dual Principles -- these are called respectively Life and Death. That which underlies the manifold workings of Destiny is called Evolution; that which produces and transforms bodily substance is called Illusion. The Creator's ingenuity is mysterious, His operations secret and profound. In truth, He is inexhaustible and eternal.

Only one who knows that Life is really Illusion, and that Death is really Evolution, can begin to learn magic from me. You and I are both illusions. How are we, then, to make a study of the subject? ... Lao Ch'eng Tsu returned home, and for three months pondered deeply over the words of the Venerable Yin Wen. Subsequently, he had the power of appearing or disappearing at will; he could reverse the order of the four seasons, produce thunderstorms in winter and ice in summer, make flying things creep and creeping things fly. But to the end of his days he never made any public display of his art.

title.en: King by Night, Slave by Day (Liezi)
title.zh: 尹氏老役夫，晝為僕，夜為君（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: Mr. Yin's estate in Chou (symbolic pin: Luoyang, Henan, China)
region.zh: 周尹氏之莊（象徵定位：河南洛陽）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: The old servant of Mr. Yin, worked mercilessly all day, dreams every night that he is a king enthroned in authority — my happiness is beyond compare, so what have I to grumble at? Mr. Yin himself, full of worldly cares, dreams every night that he is another man's servant, until his friend explains the proper balance in human destiny.
summary.zh: 周之尹氏大治產，其下趣役者侵晨昏而弗息——役夫曰：吾晝為人僕，吾夜為人君；樂樂孰加焉？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There was one old servant in particular whose physical strength had quite left him, yet his master worked him all the harder. All day long he was groaning as he went about his work, and when night came he was reeling with fatigue and would sleep like a log. His spirit was then free to wander at will, and every night he dreamt that he was a king, enthroned in authority over the multitude, and controlling the affairs of the whole State. He took his pleasure in palaces and belvederes, following his own fancy in everything, and his happiness was beyond compare.

In the daytime I am only a slave, it is true, and my misery cannot be gainsaid. But by night I am a king, and my happiness is beyond compare. So what have I to grumble at?" ... Every night he dreamt that he was another man's servant, running about on menial business of every description, and subjected to every possible kind of abuse and ill-treatment. ... "If at night you dream that you are a servant and exchange ease for affliction, that is only the proper balance in human destiny. What you want is that your dreams should be as pleasant as your waking moments. But that is beyond your power to compass."

title.en: The Wood-Cutter, the Dream-Deer, and the Magistrate (Liezi)
title.zh: 鄭人獲鹿，薪者夢鹿（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: The fuel-wood path of Chêng (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 鄭國薪樵之塗（今河南鄭州）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: A wood-cutter kills a deer, hides it in a dry ditch, and forgets the spot — becoming convinced it was all a dream. A hearer finds the deer; his wife declares it must be his own dream that has come true. The wood-cutter, dreaming that night of the real hiding-place, recovers it, and the magistrate divides the deer between them: you began by really killing a deer, but wrongly thought it was a dream.
summary.zh: 鄭人有薪於野者，遇駭鹿，御而擊之，斃之；藏諸隍中——遽而失其處，遂以為夢。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the dream-deer lawsuit became the classic Chinese dream-paradox tale. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: A man was gathering fuel in the Cheng State when he fell in with a deer that had been startled from its usual haunts. He gave chase, and succeeded in killing it. He was overjoyed at his good luck; but, for fear of discovery, he hastily concealed the carcass in a dry ditch, and covered it up with brushwood. Afterwards, he forgot the spot where he had hidden the deer, and finally became convinced that the whole affair was only a dream. He told the story to people he met as he went along; and one of those who heard it, following the indications given, went and found the deer.

"Once upon a time," he said to his wife, "a wood-cutter dreamt that he had got a deer, but couldn't remember the place where he had put it. Now I have found the deer, so it appears that his dream was a true dream." "On the contrary," said his wife, "it is you who must have dreamt that you met a wood-cutter who had caught a deer. Here you have a deer, true enough. But where is the wood-cutter? It is evidently your dream that has come true."

So the next morning, in accordance with his dream, he went to seek him out in order to recover the deer. A quarrel ensued, and the matter was finally brought before the magistrate, who gave judgment in these terms: "You began by really killing a deer, but wrongly thought it was a dream. Then you really dreamt that you had got the deer, but wrongly took the dream to be a reality. ... Meanwhile, here is the deer itself in court, and you had better divide it between you." The question was referred to the Prime Minister: "If you want to distinguish between waking and dreaming, you would have to go back to the Yellow Emperor or Confucius. But both these sages are dead, and there is nobody now alive who can draw any such distinction."

title.zh: 秦人逢氏子有忘疾，楊里華子（列子周穆王篇）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: Yang-li Hua-tzŭ of Sung is afflicted in middle age by amnesia; fortune-tellers, wizards, and physicians all fail, until the learned professor from Lu shuts himself up seven days alone with the patient — whereupon the disease disappears. And Hua-tzŭ flies into a rage: preservation and destruction, gain and loss, sorrow and joy have begun to throw out their myriad tentacles to invade my peace — oh! if I could but recapture a short moment of that blessed oblivion!
summary.zh: 宋陽里華子，中年病忘——魯儒生能治之；既愈，大怒曰：曩吾忘也，蕩蕩然——今往事之是非，哀樂嗜欲得喪，相與繆刺之若此。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Yang-li Hua-tzu, of the Sung State, was afflicted in middle age by the disease of amnesia. Anything he received in the morning he had forgotten by the evening; anything he gave away in the evening he had forgotten the next morning. Out-of-doors, he forgot to walk; indoors, he forgot to sit down. ... Fortune-tellers were summoned, but their divinations proved unsuccessful; wizards were sought out, but their exorcisms were ineffectual; physicians were called in, but their remedies were of no avail.

Then, one fine morning, the treatment came to an end, and, wonderful to relate, the disease of so many years' standing had entirely disappeared! No sooner had Hua-tzu regained his senses, however, than he flew into a great rage, drove his wife out of doors, beat his sons, and, snatching up a spear, hotly pursued the professor through the town. "Lately, when I was steeped in forgetfulness, my senses were so benumbed that I was quite unconscious of the existence of the outer world. But now I have been brought suddenly to a perception of the events of half a lifetime. Preservation and destruction, gain and loss, sorrow and joy, love and hate have begun to throw out their myriad tentacles to invade my peace. Oh! if I could but recapture a short moment of that blessed oblivion!"

title.en: The Old Man of Yen Who Wept for a Hoaxed Homeland (Liezi)
title.zh: 燕人生於燕，長於楚（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: The road from Ch'u to Yen (symbolic pin: Beijing, China)
region.zh: 楚適燕之塗（象徵定位：北京）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: A man born in Yen and brought up in Ch'u returns to his native country in old age; his fellow-travellers hoax him through the Chin State — the capital of Yen! your village altar! your ancestors' tomb! — until he weeps aloud, then they laugh: this is only the Chin State. When he really does see the city and altars of Yen, his emotion is much less acute.
summary.zh: 燕人生於燕，長於楚，及老而還本國——過晉國，同行者誑之：此燕國之城、先人之廬、先人之壟——燕人大哭；眾人皆大笑。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There was once a man who, though born in Yen, was brought up in Ch'u, and it was only in his old age that he returned to his native country. On the way thither, as they were passing through the Chin State, his fellow-travellers played a practical joke on him. They pointed to the city and said: "Here is the capital of the Yen State;" whereupon the old man flushed with excitement. Pointing out a certain shrine, they told him that it was his own village altar, and he heaved a deep sigh. They showed him a house, and said: "This is where your ancestors lived;" and the tears welled up in his eyes.

Finally, they brought him in front of a mound and said: "This is the tomb where your ancestors lie buried." The old man could control himself no longer, and wept aloud. But his fellow-travellers burst into roars of laughter. "We have been hoaxing you," they cried; "this is only the Chin State." Their victim was greatly mortified; and when they arrived at their journey's end, and he really did see before him the city and altars of Yen, with the actual abode and tombs of his ancestors, his emotion was much less acute.
